I lived in Mongolia for a few years which can have -50 Celsius days and is usually quite windy. I arrived with 2 Fjallraven Parka's. One was partially goose down and partially synthetics. That really worked well. But I don't think they still produce such coats anymore. Most colleagues arrived with a Canadian Goose jacket. That ended up being worn for about two months until a better coat was found. Because in the end, none of these coats worked in the city or the Gers/Yurts. Buildings and Yurts are super hot. Buildings often 36C and Gers/Yurts can be much more. A natural Sheep lammy coat was simply the best. You would be warm in the cold, and cool enough in hot areas. Plus the coats can take a beating unlike the Canadian Goose ones. Fjallraven was very tear resistant though. But too hot in day to day circumstances. Nature still serves us best.
The Crescent Works jacket is just way too short, but also not very tear resistant if you're camping or hiking in the outdoors. Natural Lammy or Fjallraven is way better on Longevity of your coats.
The Cresent down looks nice (kind of plain looking to me though) but it definitely is cut too short for a winter jacket; it barely came to your waist.

Love my beta insulated. I live in Canada and I've been wearing it during very cold weather (-20 degrees) and it's a charm. Warm, lightweight, comfy and long enough.

In 2024 I bought an LL Bean Wind Challenger 650 fill Down Tech DWR treated ski parka. Helmet compatible, WOVEN baffles, not sewn-thru, hence the name Wind Challenger.
LOTS of good features and good to -20 F. with base layer and sweater or light fleece. As a former Nordic and later Alpine Ski Patroller I am VERY aware of what makes a good ski, winter hiking & camping parka. THIS parka meets my requirements. And don't turn your nose up at the 650 fill down. That lower fill number means LESS compressibility which is great in wind and leaning against a lift chair back, etc. If you're a mountaineer who is a gram weenie then this may not be for you but it DOES have a two way waterproof front zipper for belaying. It also has pit zips, hem drawstrings, several well designed internal and external pockets, stretch fabric for more durability and comfort, DOUBLE LAYER hood, shoulders and elbows to wrist, etc.

The problem with these jackets is that they snag on a tree branch and are completely ruined after that. That's why I went with the Carhartt Montana or the Carhartt Yukon extremes coat with cordera nylon. $150 will buy you the carhart Montana and $200 will buy you the Yukon extreme's jacket with the corduroy collar.

The arcteryx was too warm for me, even in -20 and beyond weather and also doesn't layer with hoodies, which is a no go to me. I've found that layering myself in more layers than one might otherwise need and using wool or less insulating synthetic jackets has worked perfectly for me. I took a Crescent Down jacket, yes, it looked absolutely insane and I adored it for that. Unfortunately, it was absolutely useless in any scenario outside of fashion.


Its design is very short like a trucker jacket, you lose a lot of heat moving around and bending over and your lower back gets very cold. The smallest random embers from a fire tear through it and make it like swiss cheese. Honestly I couldn't even see these embers floating around but the next day the jacket was riddled in tiny burn holes. The jacket was also so breathable, the super puffy down was wasted, you end up having a really bulky, snag prone jacket that is only as warm as something half its thickness.
